sweep_summary: One item for Cheyenne: Frantz 1972b 'The origin of Cheyenne pitch accent' (IJAL 38(4):223-225, DOI 10.1086/465218 confirmed via Crossref). Closed access everywhere checked (Unpaywall/OpenAlex/Semantic Scholar closed; journals.uchicago.edu and JSTOR blocked; no author page found; archive.org holds the issue only as a borrow-only microfilm scan whose text derivatives could not be reached by automated download). Readable evidence obtained: (a) the published abstract in Maddieson & Gandour 1974, An Annotated Bibliography on Tone (UCLA WPP 28, ERIC ED101587, open PDF, entry 9132, p. 44), and (b) uncorrected-scanned snippets of pp. 223-224 via archive.org's public full-text search, saved to the target directory. The note argues that Cheyenne 'pitch accent' (lexically inherent high pitch plus rule-derived alternations) is the reflex of Proto-Algonquian vowel length; it states no positional word-stress rule, and its own data show multiple high syllables per word. It refines rather than contradicts the catalog's 'tonal' coding: Leman 1981 (IJAL 47:283-309, snippets also read and saved) and the catalog's Leman grammar explicitly reject the pitch accent label while accepting Frantz's historical claim. Best new first-hand statement read: Leman 1981 sec. 2 ('two phonemic pitches, or tones, high and low'; a separate stress system, if any, is 'very minor'), which confirms but does not supersede the catalog's deciding source. new_statements.quote: Cheyenne also has two contrastive tones: high, which is marked with an acute accent in this paper, and low, which is not marked here, consistent with the orthography. [p. 3] ... The fact that the penultimate syllable is the only position in the word that resists a domain-span process of vowel devoicing when all segmental and tonal conditions are met suggests that it has a privileged status relative to the rest of the word. While Cheyenne is not a canonical stress language, I propose that the resistance to devoicing in the penultimate syllable reflects word-level prominence in that position (consistent with arguments in Milliken 1983 and Bogomolets 2019). new_statements.rule_in_words: Cheyenne has two contrastive tones (high, low). It is 'not a canonical stress language'; the author proposes an abstract word-level prominence on the underlying penultimate syllable (counted before word-final <e> epenthesis, so the surface antepenult in words with an epenthetic final [e]), diagnosed solely by that syllable's resistance to prepenultimate vowel devoicing. No phonetic stress cue and no placement rule beyond 'penult' is given.
new_statements.exceptions: Prominence is computed on the underlying, pre-epenthesis penult: in words ending in epenthetic [e] the surface antepenultimate syllable is the one that resists devoicing (ex. 19, p. 6, citing Leman and Rhodes 1978). The general typological sentence on p. 2 ('while it may be blocked by suprasegmental properties such as stress or high tone') is about devoicing cross-linguistically, not a Cheyenne stress claim.
new_statements.identity_note: Vogel 2021 describes Cheyenne 'spoken in Montana and Oklahoma' using data from Leman's grammar (1980, 2011), Leman and Rhodes 1978 and the Fisher et al. 2017 dictionary, i.e. essentially the Northern Cheyenne (Montana) material of the SIL tradition; no dialect split is drawn. Frantz 1972b (SIL) gives no dialect identification in the readable snippets. Nothing describes another language or variety.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Frantz treats Cheyenne as one of several Algonquian 'pitch accent' systems in which pitch functions as an accent or stress; high-pitched syllables (marked with the acute) are the 'pitch accent' syllables, and he notes that Davis 1962's 'every vowel has either high or low tone' is a descriptively equivalent formulation. Some accents are derived by ordered rules (accent shifts under suffixation), others are 'inherent accent' fixed in position (e.g. badger ma?héhko?e sg. / pl.), which he derives historically from Proto-Algonquian vowel length; the remaining 'rules of accent alternation' are 'ill-understood'. No fixed-position word-stress rule is stated.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any readable snippet.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent shifts when suffixes are added (rule-derived accents) versus 'inherent accent' whose position is permanent; 'apparent exceptions' and 'ill-understood rules of accent alternation' (p. 224) are acknowledged but not resolved. Caution: the 'stress' snippets in the older snippet file that read '(4) a. Stress every noun or verb stem. b. Stress the first syllable of every particle.. stems have a fixed stress.. prefixes have a variable stress' come from a different article in the same IJAL 38(4) issue, not from Frantz's Cheyenne paper, and must not be attributed to Cheyenne.

tone_statements.quote: Appendix. In this brief section we would like to outline in a rough way the basics of the Cheyenne tone system as we understand them. A more definitive statement is forthcoming (Leman, in preparation). There are two independent prosodic systems operating in Cheyenne: one of pitch and one of stress. Our understanding of stress is very limited at this time, but it appears that the basic rule stresses every other voiced syllable starting from the right with the last voiced syllable which gets the loudest stress. The rule seems to be restarted from the preverb boundary. [...] The vowel clusters eo [eyo] and oa [owa] act as two syllables with respect to the stress rule, all other vowel clusters act as a single syllable with respect to this rule. [...] Our understanding of pitch phenomena is also somewhat limited, but we can say the following things. While there are only two underlying tones, high and low, there are numerous phonetically different pitch levels due to the action of two rules which lower high tones following low tones. readall_conflicts: Two disagreements, both partly terminological. (1) Type label: Frantz 1972b calls Cheyenne a 'pitch accent' system in which pitch functions as an accent or stress; Leman 1981 (already in the catalog's existing statement) and Vogel 2021 call it a two-tone (high/low) language, and Leman explicitly rejects Frantz's label because more than one syllable per word carries the tonal contrast. Frantz concedes the 'every vowel has either high or low tone' description is equivalent. (2) Existence and place of stress: the catalog's grammar line 'There is no word stress (accent), as in English' and Leman 1981's 'if there is a separate stress system, its role is very minor' stand against Vogel 2021 (with Milliken 1983 and Bogomolets 2019), who proposes an abstract word-level prominence on the underlying penultimate syllable, diagnosed only by resistance to prepenultimate devoicing; Vogel herself says Cheyenne is 'not a canonical stress language', so this is a phonological-prominence claim rather than a phonetic stress placement, and it does not overturn the tonal coding. No new text was opened, so no new conflict arises. The standing disagreement held by the project is terminological: Frantz 1972b (read earlier only as search snippets) calls the Cheyenne system 'pitch accent', while the catalog's deciding sources (Leman 2023 grammar; Leman 1981 IJAL) code Cheyenne as a tone language with no word stress and explicitly reject the pitch accent label because more than one syllable per word ca…

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding passages are verbatim in the Leman grammar text we hold at the stated pages (footers 34/35 and 47/48). (2) Deciding source is the current reference grammar by the language's principal describer (draft 2026, lineage 1979-2021, top of Glottolog's grammar list), who also authored the IJAL phonology article on Cheyenne pitch; it states twice that Cheyenne is a tone language without word stress and not pitch accent. No instrumental stress study exists. (3) Web search surfaced a theoretical counter-tradition (Frantz 1972 pitch accent; Milliken 1983 and Vogel 2021/2022 abstract penultimate 'accent'/prosodic head inferred from devoicing and coalescence blocking, with Milliken conceding no phonetic evidence). I downloaded Milliken 1983 (Zenodo) and Vogel 2022 (Cornell eCommons) to; both confirm the high/low tone contrast

Our understanding of stress is very limited at this time, but it appears that the basic rule stresses every other voiced syllable starting from the right with the last voiced syllable which gets the loudest stress. The rule seems to be restarted from the preverb boundary. [...] The vowel clusters eo [eyo] and oa [owa] act as two syllables with respect to the stress rule, all other vowel clusters act as a single syllable with respect to this rule. [...] Our understanding of pitch phenomena is also somewhat limited, but we can say the following things. While there are only two underlying tones, high and low, there are numerous phonetically different pitch levels due to the action of two rules which lower high tones following low tones. Vogel 2021), and thus may be considered analogous to stress.' (pp. 71-72). Based on Leman & Rhodes 1978, Leman 1980/2011, Fisher et al. 2017; no phonetic measurement of stress.

sources.quote: Cheyenne also has two contrastive tones: high, which is marked with an acute accent in this paper, and low, which is not marked here, consistent with the orthography. [p. 3] ... The fact that the penultimate syllable is the only position in the word that resists a domain-span process of vowel devoicing when all segmental and tonal conditions are met suggests that it has a privileged status relative to the rest of the word. While Cheyenne is not a canonical stress language, I propose that the resistance to devoicing in the penultimate syllable reflects word-level prominence in that position (consistent with arguments in Milliken 1983 and Bogomolets 2019). [pp. 6-7]

sources.quote: [p.223 §1] 'A number of Algonkian languages have pitch-accent systems in which pitch functions as an accent or stress, though some investigators have referred to these as two-[tone systems] ... [fn.1] Haas 1936 reports a pitch accent for Penobscot; Day 1964 says that Abnaki has two levels of stress' [§2] 'Clearly, Cheyenne has distinctive surface pitch patterns; compare the following pairs, in which relatively high pitched syllables have acute accent; these are the syllables with "pitch accent" ... hétame dog hotáme dogs. And while some pitch patterns can be accounted for by ordered phonological rules, as suggested by the frequent shift of accent when suffixes are added ..., there apparently are certain vowels which must be assigned inherent accent in order for the rules to work; note the permanence of the accent position in the word badger: ma?héhko?e (sg.) ...' [fn] '...locution of saying that every vowel has either high or low tone.' [§3] 'the reflex of PA vowel length in Cheyenne is the inherent accent discussed briefly in 2.' sources.quote: Cheyenne has two distinctive (phonemic) pitches: 1. high (marked with the acute accent, as in á) 2. low (unmarked) It also has three variations of these two pitches, which can be accounted for by the pitch rules described in my IJAL article of 1981 ...: 3. raised high (... now marked with the regular high pitch mark) 4. mid pitch (marked with the macron, as in ē) 5. lowered high (now with no mark) Here are pairs of Cheyenne words which differ only in the pitch (tone) on their vowels
